description: I am Abhishek V, a computer science engineering student. I am highly interested in astronomy and space. That is why I participated in this hackathon.
summary:
SPACE RELICS – The Museum Beyond Earth is an interactive digital museum and space archaeology platform developed by Team Orange Army for the NASA International Space Apps Challenge.

Addressing the theme "Abandoned but not Forgotten," our platform documents humanity’s mechanical pioneers across the Moon and Mars—including Apollo descent stages, pioneering rovers (Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity), and discarded landing hardware. Built with React and Three.js, it features interactive 3D WebGL celestial globes with verified sub-meter NASA coordinates, a "Then vs. Now" orbital forensic comparison tool using LROC and HiRISE imagery, an educational detective quiz, and an 8-part archaeological dossier with first-person "If This Object Could Talk" audio monologues.

This project is crucial because over 210,000 kg of human equipment rests on other worlds, too often dismissed as mere "space trash." As commercial exploration and the Artemis era accelerate, SPACE RELICS redefines these artifacts as sacred monuments of human curiosity and scientific sacrifice, preserving our extraterrestrial cultural heritage for future generations.
details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?

SPACE RELICS – The Museum Beyond Earth is an interactive educational digital museum that catalogs, maps, and tells the stories of human-made equipment abandoned on the Moon and Mars.

The application operates through several interconnected modules:

  • Interactive 3D Planetary Explorer: Built with Three.js, users navigate WebGL 3D celestial globes of the Moon and Mars with procedural shaders and atmospheric glows. Landing pins are calculated via spherical trigonometry from real NASA landing coordinates (x,y,zx, y, zx,y,z). It also offers a 2D Equirectangular Projection Grid distinguishing verified sub-meter laser coordinates from approximate Doppler estimates.
  • Searchable Artifact Museum: A multi-parameter catalog featuring rovers, descent stages, scientific packages (ALSEP retroreflectors), and EDL hardware (sky cranes, parachutes). Users can filter by celestial body, equipment category, mission era, and operational status.
  • 8-Part Archaeological Storytelling: Each artifact features an exhaustive historical dossier chronicling its journey, engineering purpose, why it remained behind, and its modern condition.
  • "IF THIS OBJECT COULD TALK": Features dramatized first-person monologues grounded strictly in telemetric data, complete with a built-in browser speech synthesis audio narrator.
  • "Then vs. Now" Forensics: An interactive before/after split-view slider that juxtaposes original ground mission photography against modern orbital reconnaissance from NASA’s LROC and MRO HiRISE.
  • Mission Detective Quiz & Saved Collection: A gamified 4-category challenge with streak counters, celebratory confetti, and unlockable heritage badges, along with a localStorage museum field pass that visitors can export as a JSON dossier.
  • Live NASA API Search: Real-time integration with images-api.nasa.gov allowing visitors to query NASA’s master photography library.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Accessible STEM Education: Bridges the gap between complex orbital telemetry and accessible, emotionally engaging storytelling for K-12 students and the general public.
  • Zero Barrier to Entry: Runs 100% locally in the browser with zero paid subscriptions, third-party paywalls, or mandatory API keys.
  • Scientific Integrity: Replaces speculative "space junk" rhetoric with verified NASA datasets, teaching users how orbital cameras (LROC, HiRISE) actually detect surface artifacts and what resolution limits mean.
  • Active Heritage Awareness: Connects historic space exploration with modern space law, helping users understand why protecting landing sites is critical for the Artemis era.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The intended impact is to shift global perception from viewing discarded hardware as "space trash" to recognizing them as irreplaceable monuments of human civilization and cultural heritage. As commercial spaceflight and national return missions to the Moon and Mars surge, historic sites (such as Tranquility Base or Endeavour Crater) face real risks of contamination and physical damage. By popularizing space archaeology, SPACE RELICS fosters stewardship for our extraterrestrial heritage under frameworks like the Artemis Accords (Section 9) and the 1967 Outer Space Treaty.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Development Platform & Prototyping: Google Antigravity (used by Team Orange Army for rapid full-stack architecture, agentic data integration, and NASA API pipeline validation).
  • Frontend Framework: React 18 with TypeScript for strict type safety.
  • Build Tooling: Vite for fast bundling and hot module replacement.
  • 3D Visualizations & WebGL: Three.js for procedural 3D celestial globes and coordinate mapping.
  • Styling & UI: Tailwind CSS (custom cosmic dark mode, scanlines, glassmorphism) and Lucide Icons.
  • Browser APIs: Web Speech API (SpeechSynthesis) for relic audio monologues and localStorage for curated field dossiers and badge persistence.
  • Interactive Animations: canvas-confetti for celebratory gamification feedback.
  • NASA Data Sources: NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDC), Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC), Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (HiRISE), NASA Image and Video Library Public API, and the Apollo Lunar Surface Journals (ALSJ).

5. How is your project creative?

  • First-Person Telemetric Monologues: Instead of dry technical spreadsheets, relics narrate their own stories in "IF THIS OBJECT COULD TALK" (e.g., Spirit describing dragging its stuck wheel to discover hot-spring silica, or the Apollo 11 laser reflector recounting 50+ years of returning photon pulses).
  • Dual-View Orbital Forensics: The interactive split slider empowers users to act as orbital forensic scientists, comparing historic astronaut camera angles with contemporary satellite passes.
  • Audio Atmosphere & Multi-Sensory Immersion: Integrated speech narration allows visitors to listen to the artifacts speak while inspecting their 3D landing coordinates.
  • Gamified Space Detective: Turns archival telemetry clues into an interactive mystery game that rewards learning with collectible heritage badges.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Scientific Truth vs. Artistic Dramatization: We strictly avoided inventing coordinates, dates, or outcomes. Where telemetry is approximate (e.g., Soviet Luna 9), it is explicitly badged as such. Fictionalized monologues are explicitly labeled as dramatized educational monologues grounded in real mission telemetry.
  • Accessibility & Performance: We implemented automated image fallback systems (onError handlers) so that network throttling or CDN blocks never display broken images.
  • Space Law & Cultural Preservation: We integrated international treaties (Outer Space Treaty Art. VIII, Artemis Accords Sec. 9) to ensure the project teaches ethical stewardship of interplanetary sites.
  • Device Responsiveness: Designed with responsive desktop and mobile HUD interfaces, ensuring fluid 3D interactions whether accessed on a classroom tablet or desktop workstation.
